video_title: Robotic Deep-Dive: Beating China, the Race Against Tesla, & New Robotics Timeline With Brett Adcock
gist: Brett Adcock, founder of Figure (and the AI company Hark), tells Peter Diamandis and co-host Dave that humanoids are in the 'flip phone era': Helix 2.5 already zero-shots unseen homes and warehouses with log-linear data scaling, the undertrained Helix 3 is a 'baby AGI' moment, and Figure 4 (with near-human hands, designed for lights-out self-manufacture) will be the 'iPhone one moment', with full home capability expected before end-2027. He says compute ran out globally in September 2026, memory makers have no humanoid capacity, China (not Tesla) is the main rival, and argues AI-native devices will displace the iPhone while Hark may soon surpass Figure in size.

insights.claim: Brett Adcock frames the humanoid race in four chapters: (1) functional, affordable hardware at volume, (2) an end-to-end neural-net AI recipe for long-horizon loco-manipulation, (3) scaling intelligence via data and compute, and (4) scaling robot production; he says Figure has finished chapter 2 and is now in chapter 3.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Use the four-chapter lens to stage-gate humanoid companies: most competitors are still proving chapter 1-2, so valuation premiums should track demonstrated data/compute scaling, not demos.
insights.quote: chapter three and four for me are like scaling intelligence and scaling robots.

insights.claim: Figure will not ship a home robot until it is an 'Apple-style' quality product that works without teleoperation or failures for a dozen-plus hours a day, and Adcock predicts competitors that launch earlier will fail the way Humane and Rabbit did in AI devices.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Expect early teleoperated home-humanoid launches from rivals to disappoint; Figure's consumer revenue will lag commercial revenue by design.
insights.quote: You've seen this now with Humane and Rabbit and these other groups in the in the AI device space.

insights.claim: Figure is testing in 20 to 100 net-new California homes at any given time; Adcock hopes within roughly six months to drop a robot into any unseen home and complete long-horizon tasks over hours, and says he would be 'very shocked' if the full home picture is not demonstrated before the end of 2027.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Sets a dated milestone (zero-shot long-horizon home work by end-2027) to track Figure against; consumer sales would follow later after safety/reliability work.
insights.quote: I'd be very shocked if we exit 2027. We haven't seen this this whole picture.

insights.claim: Adcock calls the first undertrained checkpoint of Helix 3, shown in Figure's secret 'Blackbox' home lab, a 'baby AGI' moment: an adult robot body with roughly a two-year-old's intelligence that attempts arbitrary open-ended prompts, with much larger models already in evaluation.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Signals a step change in general-purpose robot policy capability is coming in the next model releases; watch for public Helix 3 demos as a catalyst.
insights.quote: it feels for me like a really like a baby agi moment

insights.claim: Helix 2.5 performed zero-shot household work (making beds, tidying living rooms) in 30 rented homes never seen in training, and Figure reports what it believes are the first humanoid data scaling laws: a log-linear improvement in model loss and real-world task execution as data increases.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: If robotics follows LLM-style scaling laws, capital (data + compute) becomes the moat, favoring the best-funded humanoid players and GPU suppliers.
insights.quote: we also showed the first like what we think is the first humanoid scaling laws for data.

insights.claim: About three weeks before the interview Figure took a robot to a new client warehouse it had never seen and the Helix 2.5 model zero-shotted the logistics task despite different lighting, conveyors and package mix; Adcock says a year earlier he would have expected this to take up to five years.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Zero-shot deployment collapses integration cost per commercial site, which is the key driver of humanoid unit economics in logistics.

insights.claim: Figure's logistics robots have run practically every day on a package line since a roughly 200-hour live stream about four months before the interview, needing sub-3-second package handling with only a few percent errors per shift.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Continuous-operation track records are the evidence commercial buyers need; this is the proof point behind Figure's commercial pipeline.

insights.claim: Adcock says consumer home robots will need a roughly $300-$500 per month lease (about $10 a day) and he leans toward leasing because it lowers upfront cost and lets owners get the newest generation every few years as hardware improves quickly; Diamandis says audiences typically say they would own at least two.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Robots-as-a-service economics imply a large consumer financing/lease market and recurring revenue rather than one-off hardware sales.
insights.quote: you'll need some sort of like $300 to $500 a month lease.

insights.claim: Figure will keep robot maintenance and repair in-house during the initial ramp to guarantee experience quality, though Adcock says the end state is not Figure doing everything.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Early service costs sit on Figure's P&L; third-party service networks are a later-stage opportunity.

insights.claim: Adcock says humanoids are in the 'flip phone era' and that Figure 4 will be an 'iPhone one moment' and the largest generational step up Figure has ever made, making Figure 3 (which he calls the best humanoid on the market) 'look like a caveman'.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Figure 4 launch is a major catalyst; buyers of current-gen humanoids face fast obsolescence, which supports a lease model.
insights.quote: Figure 4 is probably like iPhone one moment we're going to have here soon.

insights.claim: Figure has built seven iterations of its robot hand over about two years, including both tendon-driven and non-tendon-driven designs, and Adcock claims a gloved Figure 4 hand will be almost indistinguishable from a gloved human hand.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Human-level dexterity is the gating capability for most blue-collar and manufacturing tasks; a credible hand step-change widens the addressable task set.
insights.quote: a figure 4 with a glove and a human with a glove is almost indistinguishable.

insights.claim: Figure 4 was explicitly designed to enable closed-loop 'lights-out' manufacturing that Figure 3's design made difficult, with Adcock saying it is the robot that will 'build itself'; he is confident full lights-out manufacturing arrives within five years but unsure whether that is 6 months or 3 years away.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Robots building robots would drive exponential unit-cost declines and production ramps; watch for documented self-assembly demos.
insights.quote: part of this is like we think this is the robot that will like build itself

insights.claim: Figure vertically integrates actuators, hands and touch sensing because off-the-shelf parts failed: the best elbow actuator on the market was three times too big, three times overweight and cost hundreds of dollars when Figure needs tens of dollars per unit.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Component suppliers are not yet built for humanoid cost/size targets, so integrated players capture margin while component vendors risk being designed out.
insights.quote: we can't have it hundreds of dollars. It needs to be like tens of dollars at the most.

insights.claim: Figure's BotQ facility can produce maybe over 40,000 humanoids a year at full rate across four lines, which Adcock says will not be enough; an unannounced new manufacturing facility is in the works and he sees a path to a million units a year from a facility if chapter-3 intelligence problems are solved.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Implies a large capex cycle (and likely more fundraising or an eventual IPO) tied to solving general-purpose intelligence.
insights.quote: we can do you know like maybe over 40,000 or so units now at full rate at a Baku next door a year across like four lines.

insights.claim: Figure now has well over 1,000 (roughly 1,500) robots on campus versus about 700-800 employees, having crossed more robots than humans four to five months before the interview, and spends about a year between hardware programs.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: A gauge of current production run-rate and internal dogfooding scale.

insights.claim: Figure rotated its supply chain out of Chinese piece parts after tariffs spiked (one week it paid 270% tariffs) and geopolitical tension rose, and Adcock says it is now in very good shape on that front.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: US humanoid makers de-risking from China supports domestic component suppliers and reduces tariff exposure in BOM costs.
insights.quote: I think at one point like last year we were paying like one one week was like 270% tariffs.

insights.claim: Figure signed a deal with nscale for second-half-2027 compute that the hosts describe as 100,000 GPUs for $3B+ on Vera Rubin chips, which Adcock estimates at well over 100x Figure's current compute; Figure was also doubling internal compute the week of the interview.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Robotics labs are becoming hyperscale GPU buyers, adding a new demand vector for Nvidia and neoclouds like nscale.
insights.quote: if like we took the whole uh deal with in scale and size it all the way up well over 100x what we have.

insights.claim: Figure spends low nine figures a year on compute, with about 50-70% recently going to one large Helix 3 pre-training run, and Adcock expects Figure to be doing billion-dollar training runs on Helix by next summer.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Robotics foundation-model training budgets are approaching frontier-LLM scale, raising the capital bar for competitors.
insights.quote: I expect like next summer we'll be doing billion dollar training runs on Helix.

insights.claim: Adcock says the world effectively ran out of GPU compute in September 2026: a compute RFP months earlier drew four competitive Blackwell bids that Figure negotiated down hard, but a follow-on request drew no bids and then a single bid with sellers dictating price, and even old H100s are now unavailable and 'trading above par'.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Direct evidence against the 'AI bubble/GPU glut' narrative: GPU pricing power has shifted to sellers, supportive for Nvidia, neoclouds and GPU-backed credit.
insights.quote: September 2026, the world ran out of comput. You just can't get it.

insights.claim: A C-suite of one of the world's largest memory makers told Figure it has no capacity for humanoids because all capacity is going to phones and servers, and a big memory group's CTO said humanoids are not even in their projections; Adcock says new HBM fabs take three to four years and will be oversubscribed before coming online.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Memory is the binding constraint on AI and robotics scale-up and humanoid demand is not in supplier forecasts, implying upside to memory pricing and capex.
insights.quote: we don't even have any of these in our projections.

insights.claim: Figure has struck several memory partnerships to secure memory supply for the next few years and says it is confident in near-term robot scale-up, but long-term it will need an 'unprecedented amount' of silicon.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Supply agreements are a competitive moat in a constrained memory market; smaller humanoid makers may be starved of memory.

insights.claim: Adcock is cautious about designing custom robot chips because chip programs take three-plus years and Figure's inference architecture changes too fast (Helix 3 runs in a radically different way), even though current robot chips are too costly and power-hungry; co-host Dave suggests Positron, Etched and Groq on still-available ~6nm nodes as a stopgap.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock / Dave (co-host)
insights.so_what: Robot-inference silicon is an open niche; inference-chip startups on mature nodes could win humanoid sockets before in-house chips arrive.

insights.claim: All of Figure's Helix inference, from planning and reasoning to low-level torque commands, runs onboard the robot; only real-time speech-to-speech and fleet-level agent orchestration run in the cloud because even the best 5G gives ~50 ms round trips (about 20 Hz), far too slow for millisecond-level control.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Every humanoid needs substantial onboard compute, a large edge-AI chip market, while cloud handles fleet orchestration.

insights.claim: Figure has roughly 10-15x more training data sitting on its servers than was used for the Helix 3 checkpoint, collected through a large-scale effort called 'index' to capture force and hand-interaction data the internet lacks; Adcock notes diverse data (e.g. someone painting a house) improves unrelated skills like folding laundry.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Proprietary physical-interaction data is a moat; data-collection and annotation vendors for embodied AI are a growing market.

themes.theme: Competition: China, Tesla and LLM-driven robots

insights.claim: Asked about Tesla as a competitor, Adcock says he has not seen much from Tesla in two or three years beyond some teleoperated robots.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the consensus that Tesla leads humanoids; watch Tesla's demos for genuine autonomy versus teleoperation.
insights.quote: I personally haven't seen it much out of Tesla in two or three years.

insights.claim: Adcock names 'collective China' as Figure's closest competitor given about 150 humanoid companies moving fast year to year, but says Chinese dancing/gymnastics demos use open-loop mocap-trained RL controllers that are orthogonal to general robotics, and that Unitree-style robots have no hands, weak sensors and USB-stick-sized compute.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Viral Chinese robot demos overstate general-purpose capability; the real race is in long-horizon, zero-shot autonomy, where Figure claims a lead.
insights.quote: It's a real race here.

insights.claim: Adcock argues that LLM and multimodal models shown commanding robots are not real robotics models: their demos run on fixed cameras, unlimited plugged-in compute and are sped up 5-20x to hide latency, and they cannot scale to high-dynamics full-body control.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of general AI labs' robotics demos; purpose-built robot models have a structural edge.
insights.quote: They're not real models for robotics. If they were, we would we could run them.

insights.claim: The FCC ban on importing Chinese robots shocked Adcock, who says he would prefer a level playing field, while co-host Dave reported Chinese robots bought by an MIT lab were transmitting video and audio back to China.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock / Dave (co-host)
insights.so_what: US regulatory barriers to Chinese humanoids create a protected home market for US makers despite Adcock's stated preference.

insights.claim: Figure will not do defense work because it is hard to sell robots into homes while doing military work, and Adcock believes the civilian market is hundreds to thousands of times bigger than military applications.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Figure is not a defense play; defense humanoid demand will go to other vendors.

insights.claim: Adcock says general-purpose robotics will be solved in the Bay Area or possibly Shenzhen, because a humanoid needs about 12 different engineering disciplines and SF can recruit '50 out of 50' candidates versus one or two out of 50 for Austin, Chicago or Boston.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Geography matters for humanoid startups; discount non-Bay-Area US humanoid efforts on talent access.

themes.theme: Humanoid TAM, economics and second-order effects

insights.claim: Adcock sizes the humanoid market at roughly 20 billion units: a 3.2 billion-person commercial workforce scaling to five to ten billion robots, plus at least one per human at home, operating at about a dollar an hour and creating a deeply deflationary economy.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Implies a TAM far larger than autos or phones and structural deflation in labor-intensive goods and services.
insights.quote: you're roughly like order of like 20 billion humanoids.

insights.claim: Adcock notes automation inside companies is currently bottlenecked by human shift schedules (e.g. trucks only arrive at certain times), so the next step-change comes when entire companies in logistics, healthcare or data centers run end-to-end 24/7 with robots.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: The full productivity payoff from humanoids requires redesigning whole operations, favoring firms willing to automate end-to-end.

insights.claim: Adcock argues humanoid robots are necessary to avoid a dystopia in which increasingly intelligent digital AI agents pay and direct humans to do physical work, noting TaskRabbit-style services where agents hire humans are already gaining traction.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Agent-to-human gig marketplaces are an emerging category, and a policy argument for humanoids as labor substitutes.

insights.claim: Figure sees strong demand from financiers wanting to finance its robots, mostly on commercial contracts so far, and is working with large banks and funds rather than financing robots itself, describing robot leasing as a potential multi-trillion-dollar market akin to auto leasing; no robot insurance industry has emerged yet.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Robot lease finance and robot insurance are nascent asset classes worth watching for lenders and insurers.

insights.claim: A space operator told Figure it costs low tens of millions of dollars per hour to have a human do work in space, making humanoids attractive for orbital maintenance, though Adcock admits Figure is not ready (no vacuum-rated joints).
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Space servicing is a long-dated optional market for humanoids, relevant to the maintenance objection to orbital data centers.
insights.quote: one group told us it costs like tens of like low tens of millions of dollars per hour to put a human in space to do work.

insights.claim: Figure has a large dedicated cybersecurity team and builds safety from rules in non-volatile memory up through system architecture, targeting aviation-like reliability, because a hacked robot fleet has the same risk profile as hacked self-driving cars.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Safety and security certification will be a gating factor and cost center for home humanoids.

themes.theme: Capital markets, Hark and the AI-device shift

insights.claim: Adcock says Archer Aviation went public (raising a little under $1B) only because it needed a few billion dollars for FAA certification and private capital was unavailable, that it was too young to be public and would likely still be private today if it could; he wants Figure to reach the general-robotics milestone privately, with several billion dollars of cash on the balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Do not expect a near-term Figure IPO; an eventual listing is likely after the general-robotics milestone triggers big capex needs.
insights.quote: Archer went public because we needed the money.

insights.claim: Diamandis notes Peggy Johnson just took humanoid maker Agility public, and the hosts imply it was driven by the need for capital.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Public humanoid comps are emerging; capital-driven IPOs may come early in the company life cycle, as with Archer.

insights.claim: Co-host Dave argues large public companies such as Nvidia now invest directly in fast-growing private startups, and cites roughly $9 trillion of new liquidity from Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's run-up making it possible to raise $20B for a fab in the Bay Area.
insights.speaker: Dave (co-host)
insights.so_what: Strategic corporate capital lets private AI/robotics companies stay private longer and build capex-heavy assets.

insights.claim: Adcock says Hark, his personal-intelligence AI company, saw over 1.2 million signups and about five million browser sessions in roughly a month after launching Hark Pro, had to curb some countries due to demand, is already bigger than Figure on revenue, and could be bigger than Figure overall within six months or even 90 days.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Hark is an emerging consumer AI contender to track, and a signal of Adcock's attention split across companies.
insights.quote: I bet Hark is bigger than Figure in sub six months

insights.claim: Adcock's AI-device thesis: new AI-native devices will replace the phone and computer as billion-unit-a-year 'centerpiece' devices, while accessories (like AirPods, about 3% of Apple revenue) stay single-digit revenue; he calls current Meta glasses 'horrible' because they depend on the phone.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Bearish read-through for incumbent smartphone platforms and for accessory-style AI wearables; bullish for whoever owns the new AI centerpiece device.
insights.quote: there will be AI devices that will kill those in the middle.

insights.claim: Adcock argues Apple has lost so much momentum on AI that roughly a year ago it crossed a point where it is too hard to turn around, and predicts that in about 10 years people will not use a traditional phone.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: A contrarian long-term bear case on Apple's iPhone franchise from a builder of AI devices.
insights.quote: the iPhone's going to go away

insights.claim: Adcock says OpenAI co-led Figure's Series B with Microsoft and joined its board, but the AI collaboration was lopsided (Figure making 10-to-1 to 100-to-1 the progress) and OpenAI staff rarely visited, so Figure ended the partnership about two years ago; he believes OpenAI then wanted to get back into robotics.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: OpenAI is a likely future humanoid competitor; partnerships between AI labs and robot makers carry IP-leakage risk.

insights.claim: Figure and Hark believe real-time speech-to-speech is the default UI layer for robots and AI hardware; Figure's robots use Hark's in-house speech model, and Adcock says current industry speech-to-speech is poor at latency, interruption and tool calling.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Voice-native interfaces are a key battleground for AI devices and robots; in-house voice models are a differentiator.

insights.claim: Adcock says that apart from the FCC ban on Chinese humanoids in the prior 90 days, Figure has seen no regulatory moves aimed at humanoid robots, unlike the debate over superintelligence and calls from figures like Bernie Sanders to slow AI.
insights.speaker: Brett Adcock
insights.so_what: Humanoid regulation risk is currently low but could emerge as robots enter public spaces.
